t.1.206.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: As that mighty-armed one, the bringer of glory to the Kauravas, set out, great-souled brahmins who had mastered the Vedas followed him.
t.1.206.2: Men learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and likewise those who meditate on the supreme self, pure devotees of the Blessed Lord, and those who were bards and reciters of the Purāṇas.
t.1.206.4: Surrounded by these and by many other companions of gentle speech, the son of Pāṇḍu set forth, like Vāsava surrounded by the Maruts.
t.1.206.3: And other storytellers too, O king, and ascetics dwelling in the forest, and those twice-born who sweetly recite divine tales.
t.1.206.6: And he saw the holy tīrthas, O bull among the Bhāratas; having reached Gaṅgādvāra, the lord made his encampment there.
t.1.206.5: He saw lovely and wondrous forests and lakes, rivers and seas, and many lands as well, O Bhārata.
t.1.206.8: When the son of Kuntī and the brāhmaṇas had settled there, O Bhārata, those priests kindled their agnihotra fires in great numbers.
t.1.206.7: Hear from me, Janamejaya, the wondrous deed that he, the pure-souled foremost chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍavas, performed there.
t.1.206.10: O king, that Gaṅgādvāra shone exceedingly with those great-souled, learned men, self-restrained and standing on the path of the good, who had performed their ablutions.
t.1.206.9: When those fires were being kindled and were blazing, when oblations had been poured into them and offerings of flowers had been made, and when they stood along the different stretches of the riverbank,
t.1.206.11: While that encampment was thus astir, the son of Pāṇḍu, the son of Kuntī, went down into the Gaṅgā to bathe.
t.1.206.12: Having bathed there and offered libations to his forefathers, he was about to climb out of the water, O king, wishing to perform the fire rite.
t.1.206.13: O great king, the mighty-armed one was drawn down into the depths of the water by Ulūpī, the daughter of the king of the Nāgas, who desired him.
t.1.206.14: There, in the supremely honored abode of the Nāga Kauravya, the Pāṇḍava saw a well-kindled fire, carefully prepared.
t.1.206.16: Then, having performed the fire-rite, the son of Kuntī, as if smiling, spoke these words to the daughter of the king of the Nāgas.
t.1.206.15: There Dhanaṃjaya, the son of Kuntī, performed the fire rite; and Hutāśana, receiving oblations from him who offered them without any misgiving, was well pleased.
t.1.206.17: What is this rash deed you have done, timid one, O beautiful lady? And what is this lovely land, who are you, and whose daughter are you?
t.1.206.18: Ulūpī said: Born in the lineage of Airāvata is a serpent named Kauravya; I am his daughter, O Pārtha, a serpent-maiden named Ulūpī.
t.1.206.19: I am that very one, O Kaunteya, who, merely upon seeing you descend into the sea-bound river to bathe, have been made faint by Kandarpa.
t.1.206.20: Me, who am thus tormented by Anaṅga for your sake and devoted to no other, O joy of the Kurus, delight today in private by the gift of yourself.
t.1.206.21: Arjuna said: This twelve-year vow of celibacy of mine, gentle lady, has been enjoined by the King of Dharma; I am not my own master.
t.1.206.22: And I too wish to do what is pleasing to you, O water-dweller; yet never before at any time has any untruth been spoken by me.
t.1.206.23: How might that not be a falsehood, and yet also be pleasing to you, and my dharma not be harmed? So would I act, O serpent maiden.
t.1.206.24: I know, son of Pāṇḍu, how you are wandering over the earth, and how your elder has enjoined this vow of celibacy upon you.
t.1.206.26: So this banishment of one another on account of Draupadī has been established by you for the sake of dharma; in this, dharma is not violated.
t.1.206.25: Whoever of us, out of folly, should intrude upon another of us while he is with Drupada's daughter, he among us shall live a life of celibacy in the forest for twelve years: such was the compact made by you.
t.1.206.27: The distressed must be given protection, O wide-eyed one. By granting me protection, your dharma is not violated.
t.1.206.28: Or even if there should be some subtle transgression of this dharma, it would still be dharma for you, Arjuna, for you would have given me my life.
t.1.206.30: By granting me life, O mighty-armed one, practise the highest dharma; I have come to you today for refuge, O best of men.
t.1.206.29: Accept me, who am devoted to you, Pārtha; this is the opinion of the good, my lord. If you will not do so, know that I am dead.
t.1.206.32: Filled with desire, I entreat you; therefore do what is dear to me. By giving yourself to me, you ought to fulfill my desire.
t.1.206.31: O Kaunteya, you always protect the wretched and the helpless; so I come to you for refuge, and in my sorrow I cry out again and again.
t.1.206.33: Thus addressed by the daughter of the lord of serpents, the son of Kuntī did all of that just as she asked, taking dharma as his reason.
t.1.206.34: Having spent that night in the abode of the Nāgas, the mighty one rose and set out from Kauravya's dwelling when the sun had risen.
